trivia: Women here only got the right to vote in 1970, and the right to run as candidates themselves came three years later, in 1973. Yet in 2011 I became the first country in Europe to elect a parliament with more women than men: 15 of the 28 seats.
My national anthem is written as if I, the country, am singing it. It opens with 'The great Charlemagne, my father', and calls me the only remaining daughter of his empire.

In the Casa de la Vall, my old stone parliament house, stands a cupboard with seven locks. It held my most precious documents. Each of my seven parishes kept one of the keys, so it could only be opened when all seven were there together.

trivia: My patron saint, Our Lady of Meritxell, was a 12th-century wooden statue of the Virgin. In 1972, on the night of her feast day, her chapel burned down with the statue inside, and the Barcelona architect Ricardo Bofill then built her a brand-new basilica.

trivia: My national day, 8 September, honours Our Lady of Meritxell, a statue of the Virgin, rather than a battle or a revolution. My national anthem was first sung in the cathedral on that same day in 1921.
My best-loved mountain dish, trinxat, is cabbage and potato mashed together and fried with bacon into a crisp cake. Cooks wait for cabbage that has been touched by frost, because it tastes sweeter.
My national stew is a winter feast in one pot: chicken, veal, meatballs, pig's snout and trotters and sausage, cooked with cabbage, potatoes, beans and giant pasta shells.
My biggest ski area, Grandvalira, has about 215 km of slopes, the largest in the Pyrenees. Linked with my two other resorts, the total passes 300 km, all inside a country smaller than many cities.
My national football team lost its first 30 competitive matches. Win number 31 finally came in October 2004, 1–0 against North Macedonia, with a second-half volley from defender Marc Bernaus.

My national flower, the grandalla or poet's daffodil, covers high meadows every spring with white petals and a little yellow cup rimmed in red. In 2021 it even got its own €1.25 coin, a special edition of just 3,000 made for coin collectors rather than for spending.
My capital sits at 1,023 metres above sea level, which makes it the highest capital city in Europe.
Every bit of me is mountain: 65 peaks, the tallest being Coma Pedrosa at 2,942 m, and an average elevation of almost 2,000 metres. I am also landlocked between just two neighbours, France and Spain.

My only World Heritage Site, the Madriu-Perafita-Claror Valley, is a glacial valley covering about a tenth of my territory, with shepherds' huts, terraced fields and old iron forges. It is the one part of me with no roads at all.
In Escaldes-Engordany, an 80-metre glass spire, my tallest building, crowns Caldea, the largest thermal spa in southern Europe, fed by natural hot springs.

In Canillo, a Tibetan-style footbridge just 1 metre wide stretches 603 metres across a mountain valley and hangs up to 158 metres above the river. When it opened in 2022 it was among the longest of its kind in the world.

My two heads of state are the President of France and a Catholic bishop from across the border in Spain. So French voters choose one of my princes, and the Pope appoints the other. Yet I am not French territory: the princes' role is mostly ceremonial, and my own parliament and prime minister run the country.

trivia: Visitors leave with bags of cheap tobacco, alcohol and perfume from Avinguda Meritxell and the border shops. My 4.5% sales tax beats Spain's 21% VAT, so prices run 20–40% lower, and customs checks enforce allowances on the way out.
I use the euro but only got the right to mint my own coins in the 2010s, so collectors snap them up. My 1-euro coin shows the Casa de la Vall, my old stone parliament house.
